title: From ARPANET to the Web
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: In just over half a century, the internet has changed from an experiment connecting a handful of computers into a network used by more than five billion people, about two thirds of the world's population. It has altered the way we work, learn, shop, travel and communicate with friends. Many people use it every hour without knowing how it works, or that it was created by a small group of scientists who could not have imagined its size. This passage describes the main steps in its development, explains the difference between the internet and the web and considers some of the problems that it has created.

The story begins in 1969, when American researchers connected four university computers in a project called ARPANET. The aim was to let scientists share expensive machines and to build a network that would continue to work even if part of it were damaged. On 29 October, a student in California tried to send the first message to a computer at Stanford, 560 kilometres away. He typed only two letters before the system crashed, so the first message sent across the network was lo, as in lo and behold. An hour later, the full message was transmitted successfully.

The network grew slowly. In 1971 an engineer, Ray Tomlinson, sent the first email between two computers and chose the symbol @ to separate the name of the user from the name of the machine, a choice that has lasted to the present day. Within a few years, email was the most popular use of the network, far more than the sharing of machines that its creators had intended. In 1983, the separate networks adopted a common set of rules, called TCP/IP, which allowed them to exchange data. This date is often regarded as the birth of the internet, which means a network of networks.

Most people today confuse the internet with the web, but they are different things. The internet is the global system of cables, wireless links and computers that carries data. The World Wide Web is a service that runs on top of it, consisting of pages linked together and viewed by a browser. It was invented in 1989 by a British scientist, Tim Berners-Lee, who was working at CERN, the European laboratory for particle physics, and wanted a simple way for researchers to share documents. The first website went online in 1991, and in 1993 CERN announced that the technology would be free for everyone to use, a decision that made rapid growth possible.

After that, change was rapid. Easy-to-use browsers appeared in the 1990s, and search engines made it possible to find information among millions of pages. Online shops, video calls and social networks followed. In 2007 the first modern smartphones put the internet in people's pockets, and today most people reach it through a phone, not a computer. Speeds have increased enormously: a film that took hours to download in the year 2000 can now be received in seconds. At the same time, the cost has fallen, so that in many countries a connection is considered as essential as electricity or water.

The internet has also created problems. Dr Sven Lindgren, a researcher in digital society, identifies three of the most serious. First, privacy: companies collect huge amounts of data about what people read, buy and say, often without their full understanding. Second, false information: a rumour can spread around the world in minutes, long before it can be corrected. Third, inequality: about a third of humanity still has no access, especially in poor and remote regions, and they risk being left behind in education and work. He adds that the dangers are greatest for the young, who spend many hours online.

Dr Lindgren argues that the answer is not to leave the internet but to learn to use it wisely. Students should check where a piece of information comes from, compare several sources and ask who benefits from a claim before they share it. They should use strong passwords, think carefully before posting photographs and take regular breaks from screens. Many schools now teach digital literacy as a subject, alongside reading and mathematics. Dr Lindgren compares the internet to a city: it offers wonderful opportunities, but a person who walks through it without knowing the rules is likely to be hurt.
